edits.quote: Fill the sailboat and the cat. Use any small pieces.
edits.fix: As written any child finishes by covering both outlines with green triangles, and nothing tells them when they are done. Give a goal such as 'using as few pieces as you can' (fewest is 4 for the sailboat and 3 for the cat).

edits.quote: Use any small pieces.
edits.fix: The 21st Century set also has pink right triangles, teal kites and gray darts, which do not fit these triangle-grid outlines. Name the pieces children may use (green, blue, red, yellow), or print small icons of them.

edits.quote: Turn them to fit, with no gaps or overlaps.
edits.fix: This rule covers the whole activity. Move it to one unnumbered shared-rules line at the top of page 1 and take it out of P1.

edits.quote: Fill each shape two different ways.
edits.fix: Two fillings of a single-hexagon outline is trivial: the yellow hexagon alone is one of them. Rewrite as a real search, for example 'Fill the hexagon with 2 pieces, 3 pieces, 4, 5, 6 pieces', or 'find as many ways as you can', and print enough small actual-size outlines to record the answers.

edits.quote: You can use different kinds of small pieces.
edits.fix: Delete this filler sentence.

edits.quote: Ask an adult to trace your pieces before you lift them to use again.
edits.fix: Each shape is already printed twice, so children can fill both copies at once. Tracing by one adult for three children is logistics and belongs in the adult notes. On the page, say 'Draw lines to show where your pieces went.'

edits.quote: Hexagon / Diamond / First filling / Another filling (headings above the four outlines)
edits.fix: Delete these headings. The outlines need no captions.

edits.quote: Turn the pieces as needed. Use them again for the next shape.
edits.fix: Delete both sentences. The first repeats the shared rule and the second narrates how to manage the blocks.

edits.quote: Arrow outline (exactly two chevrons side by side, one possible filling)
edits.fix: The arrow is a quick entry and the star is the only real puzzle. Add an outline that chevrons cannot fill (for example the P2 hexagon or the P4 long hexagon) and ask 'Can you fill it with chevrons?'

edits.quote: Fill the long hexagon using only small blue rhombi. Then fill it again with any small pieces you like.
edits.fix: Replace the open-ended 'fill it again' add-on, which has no goal and no recording space, with 'Find all the different ways to fill the long hexagon with blue rhombi' (there are exactly 3). Print three or four small outlines to record them.

edits.quote: Fill the mountain using only small green triangles. Then fill it again with any small pieces you like.
edits.fix: Filling a 3-edge triangle with 9 green triangles is trivially easy. Use the mountain as the K-1 entry to the outline's kernel: 'Put as many blue rhombi on the mountain as you can. How many green triangles do you need to finish?' (3 blues, 3 triangles). The fewest-pieces question (3 trapezoids) works too. Drop the 'any pieces' add-on.

edits.quote: small blue rhombi / small purple chevrons / small green triangles (piece names in text only)
edits.fix: K-1 children cannot read these names. Beside each problem, print a small outline of the allowed piece so a child can check which piece to use without asking.

edits.quote: Packet ends after P5 (five quick fill-the-outline tasks)
edits.fix: A quick child finishes in about 18 minutes, so roughly 20 minutes are missing; the rewrites above recover only part of that. Add a substantial K-1 problem on the outline's idea. One option: three or four actual-size outlines, some fillable with blue rhombi and some not (equal-size even and odd shapes, a small triangle), with the question 'Which can you fill with blues? How many spaces are left on the others?'

k-1.summary: The pages are clean, actual-size, and nearly free of decoration, but every problem is a bare 'fill the outline' task with a low ceiling. Only the chevron star is a real puzzle, and nothing touches the outline's ideas (impossible fills, all the ways, fewest pieces). A quick child runs out after about 18 minutes, which is exactly the organizer's complaint that the K-1 sheet is too easy and ends too early.

edits.quote: Each blue covers two whole triangle spaces.
edits.fix: This hands children the counting idea. Restate it as a shared rule only: 'Pieces must sit exactly on the triangle spaces.'

edits.quote: Keep pieces inside the board without overlaps. / without overlaps or pieces outside / Keep pieces inside the triangle without overlaps. / Cover whole triangle spaces without overlaps or pieces outside.
edits.fix: The same rule is restated in every problem. State it once as an unnumbered shared rule at the top of page 1 and delete the repeats.

edits.quote: Boards A (9 spaces) and C (11 spaces) are the only impossible boards; Board A is identical to the 3-edge triangle in Problem 2
edits.fix: Both impossible boards fail simply because they have an odd number of spaces, and Board A duplicates P2. Replace Board A with an even-area board that has more up than down triangles, such as the 8-space trapezoid (5 up, 3 down). P1 then contrasts the odd/even reason with the up/down reason.

edits.quote: Which boards can you fill and which ones did you get stuck on? What is stopping you from completely filling some of the shapes?
edits.fix: The question is about the child's experience, not about impossibility. Rewrite as 'Which boards can be filled? For each one that cannot, explain why nobody could fill it.'

edits.quote: 2 small edges on each side / 3 small edges on each side / 4 small edges on each side / 5 small edges on each side
edits.fix: The gridded diagrams already show this. Delete the four captions.

edits.quote: Problem 2: Fit as many small blue rhombi as you can in this triangle. Keep pieces inside the triangle without overlaps. Record your best packing.
edits.fix: P2 is printed twice, with the task and rules restated and an inconsistent recording instruction. Delete the repeated heading and text and keep one statement on page 2. Alternatively, fit all four triangles under one statement.

edits.quote: Compare your four best packings. What do you notice about the number of empty spaces? Explain why you cannot leave fewer.
edits.fix: Cut the directed 'compare / what do you notice' steps. Ask the central question directly: 'For each triangle, what is the fewest number of empty spaces? Explain why no packing can leave fewer.'

edits.quote: Fewest empty triangle spaces: / Blues: ____ Purples: ____
edits.fix: In P2, 'Blues:' meant the number of pieces; here it means empty spaces. Relabel as 'Empty spaces with blues: __ with purples: __'.

edits.quote: Boards A and C (two arrows, both 0/0) and Board D (the same 10-space hexagon as Problem 1 Board D)
edits.fix: Three of the six boards give no contrast: two arrows both fill exactly, and D repeats a board from P1. Replace C and D with boards where blues and purples give different results, for example a 3-edge triangle or a 2-by-3 parallelogram. Keep B, E and F, which already contrast.

edits.quote: Can you cover one purple exactly with blues? How does this explain which pieces can leave fewer gaps?
edits.fix: The leading first question prints the method of the proof. Replace both with 'Can purples ever leave fewer empty spaces than blues on the same board? Explain.'

edits.quote: Single answer line under the closing explanation question at the bottom of a crowded page
edits.fix: Give the explanation three or four lines. Tighten the board spacing or move the question to its own space.

edits.quote: Packet ends after P3
edits.fix: A quick third grader finishes in about 30 minutes, so roughly 10 to 15 minutes are missing. Add an invention problem from the kernel, such as 'Draw a board with the same number of up and down triangles that blue rhombi still cannot fill', or 'Draw a board where blues must leave exactly 2 spaces empty', with a grid to draw on.

grades-2-3.summary: This is the strongest band. It develops the outline's coloring obstruction in sequence (impossible boards, best packings of n-edge triangles, purples never beating blues), and every board is correct and printed at actual size. The organizer would still need to remove repeated rules, the split and duplicated Problem 2, leading hint questions, duplicate and non-contrasting boards, and an ambiguous recording label. He would also need to add about one more substantial problem for quick children.

edits.quote: Find as many different tilings as you can. ... How many different tilings did you find?
edits.fix: Make 'find all' the central problem: 'Find all the tilings. How do you know there are no more?' (there are 6). As written, a child cannot tell when they are done, and the closing line only asks them to count what they found.

edits.quote: Record each blue rhombus with one line joining the centers of its two trian- gle spaces.
edits.fix: Widen the text box so 'triangle' is not hyphenated.

edits.quote: Six cards A-F showing all six tilings
edits.fix: Turning the page shows every tiling and gives away P1's answer. Have children label their own P1 recordings A-F for the map, or print the cards on a later page that adults hand out after P1.

edits.quote: Try the flip shown from A to B, then flip back.
edits.fix: Delete 'then flip back' (filler).

edits.quote: Check each line with your blocks.
edits.fix: Delete this routine checking instruction.

edits.quote: Find the shortest route from A to F. Write the cards you visit and count your flips.
edits.fix: Once the map is drawn this takes under a minute (4 flips). Fold it into P2, or enrich it: 'Which two cards are farthest apart? How many different shortest routes are there?' (2 routes, via C or via D).

edits.quote: Can you leave A and return to A in exactly three flips? Five flips? Any odd number of flips? Explain what you notice.
edits.fix: Cut the step-by-step questions and the 'explain what you notice' tic: 'Can you leave A and come back to A in an odd number of flips? Explain.'

edits.quote: Follow a ribbon from the middle of the bold bottom edge. Cross its rhombus to the middle of its opposite horizontal edge.
edits.fix: The two uses of 'its' are ambiguous. Rewrite: 'Start at the middle of the bold edge. Cross the rhombus above it to the middle of that rhombus's top edge, and keep going until you reach the top of the board.'

edits.quote: At any step, is there a choice of which rhombus to cross next? Could one tiling have two different ribbons starting at the bold edge?
edits.fix: These filler follow-ups have an obvious 'no', and the second restates the first. Delete them, or keep only the second.

edits.quote: Problem 6: Draw the ribbon on each of these tilings. Write its code from bottom to top.
edits.fix: P6 mechanically repeats P5 on four more cards and restates 'from bottom to top'. Merge P5 and P6 into one problem covering all six cards.

edits.quote: How many steps does each ribbon take? How many are L? How many are R? Use the shape of the board to explain why.
edits.fix: Replace the directed counting questions with one question: 'What do all six codes have in common? Explain using the shape of the board.'

edits.quote: Write every different order you can make with two L's and two R's. Match each order to a tiling card.
edits.fix: This unnumbered second task prints the answer to the question just above it (two L's and two R's), and its six blanks give away the count. Make it its own problem and pose the outline's payoff: 'Use the codes to explain why this board has exactly six tilings' (links back to P1).

edits.quote: Rebuild the tiling from each ribbon. Draw the four blue rhombi crossed by the ribbon, then fill the remaining spaces with blue rhombi.
edits.fix: Cut the printed method to 'Draw a tiling that has this ribbon.' Use 'Draw', not 'Rebuild': the boards are not actual size, so blocks will not fit. Both given ribbons (RLLR, LLRR) are already cards D and F, so children can copy them. Use one given ribbon plus a blank board where the child draws their own ribbon first.

edits.quote: Problem 10: Circle every neighboring RL or LR in your six codes. Can you make a flip at every circled pair? Are there any flips that do not come from one of these pairs?
edits.fix: P10 prints as a procedure the rule P9 asks children to discover, and the two overlap. Merge them: 'Find a rule that tells you, from a card's code alone, which flips it has and what the new codes are. Use your rule to explain Problem 4.' This also makes the outline's even-round-trip proof the goal, which the packet currently never connects.

grades-4-5.summary: The band develops kernel 2 faithfully and correctly: all six tiling cards, the flip demo and the ribbon examples check out (codes RRLL, RLRL, LRRL, RLLR, LRLR, LLRR, and flips swap adjacent L/R pairs), and the boards and recording space are concrete. It is split into ten mostly small, directed problems, and several of them print the next discovery (the cards reveal P1's answer, P7's second task and P10 hand over the answers). It also never asks children to use the codes for the payoffs: counting the tilings and proving that every round trip takes an even number of flips.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 pages develop the outline's up/down coloring obstruction through correct, actual-size boards, from impossible boards to n-edge triangles to purples never beating blues.
overall.weakest: The K-1 pages are five bare fill-the-outline tasks with no question beyond filling, and they run out after about 18 minutes for a quick child.
